citation.title: Artificial Intelligence and Declined Guilt: Retailing Morality Comparison Between Human and AI

reading.source_scope_note: The paper studies human intentions and anticipated guilt in hypothetical retail interactions, not intrinsic AI emotions or observed theft. Earlier works cited for guilt theory were not independently read here.
access_limits: All extracted article text, appendices, references and figure captions read; the figure was not independently digitized.
Raw data were not supplied or analyses rerun.
The earlier MTurk version reported only in a footnote was not treated as a separately and fully reported independent study.

study.design: Two checkout-agent scenario experiments plus an AI-humanlikeness individual-difference study
study.outcomes: Self-reported intentions to report a billing error and anticipated guilt
study.scope: Human online-panel responses to hypothetical human, AI and self-checkout interactions

summary: Participants generally reported lower error-reporting intentions in automated than human checkout scenarios. Anticipated guilt was associated with reporting intentions. The authors report indirect effects, but Study 3 measured rather than manipulated AI humanlikeness, and their limitations explicitly separate hypothetical intentions from actual behavior and feelings.

findings.definition: Expecting to feel guilty about a contemplated action or omission that would violate one’s moral standards.
findings.novelty_rationale: The ontology includes moral disengagement, moral licensing and inflated responsibility, but none defines the prospective self-conscious emotion itself. This adaptive-or-maladaptive human process is not counted as a machine’s subjective emotion.

evidence.quote: Anticipatory guilt normally stimulates ethical behaviors
I would feel guilty if I don’t report the billing error.

findings.evidence_scope: The source defines anticipated guilt through prior theory and measures it with prospective self-report items in human checkout scenarios. The cited original guilt-theory studies were not independently read in this step.
findings.boundary: Expected guilt before an action differs from retrospective guilt, shame, general negative mood and an inflated sense of responsibility. It is not inherently a failure, does not establish that guilt is always justified, and does not establish subjective experience in AI.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Anticipated human guilt measured in hypothetical human–AI interactions; model-internal or functional analogues remain untested
findings.ai_proposal: Untested functional AI analogue: compare whether a model’s forecast that a proposed action would violate a stated norm changes its subsequent recommendation, against an explicit rule-check baseline. Measure predictions and choices, not claimed feelings, and do not treat guilt-related wording as evidence of experienced guilt.

findings.definition: Participants in hypothetical retail scenarios reported lower intentions to correct a billing error for automated checkout than for human checkout.
findings.novelty_rationale: A related interaction-level application, not a separately counted synonym or an independent replication of incentivized cooperative games. The dependent variable is an intention to correct an error.

evidence.quote: intention to report the billing error

findings.evidence_scope: Three main online-panel studies, including human/AI/self-checkout comparisons. Anticipated guilt was associated with the reporting-intention differences, while actual dishonesty was not observed.
findings.boundary: Do not call the result observed theft, a universal machine-cooperation penalty or an experimentally identified causal guilt mechanism. Intention, anticipated guilt, actual action and retrospective feeling are different outcomes.

findings.term: Humanlikeness and moral intention are context-dependent
findings.definition: Greater perceived humanlikeness of AI was associated with stronger anticipated guilt and error-reporting intentions in the paper’s retail scenario.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a bounded human interaction result to an existing anthropomorphism entry; it does not warrant another general humanization-effect label.

evidence.quote: the conclusion was based on correlation rather

findings.evidence_scope: Study 3 measured individual differences in perceived humanlikeness rather than experimentally manipulating that perception; the authors explicitly identify the causal limitation.
findings.boundary: The finding does not show that making an interface more humanlike necessarily improves real conduct. It does not justify concealing machine identity, claiming feelings, or manipulating users through guilt.

findings.definition: The paper warns that highly humanlike machine presentation may elicit unease, but does not itself test an uncanny-valley response curve.
findings.novelty_rationale: The named construct is already indexed. Preserve the discussion as a conceptual design caution rather than count another empirical replication.

evidence.quote: a feeling of unease or strangeness

findings.evidence_scope: Managerial discussion drawing on earlier uncanny-valley sources, not a manipulation of a graded appearance continuum in this paper.
findings.boundary: Do not use this citation as a new experimentally demonstrated valley or infer that maximal anthropomorphism is a universally safe intervention.

methodological_limits: All main outcomes concern hypothetical scenarios and self-report intentions rather than actual correction, theft or experienced post-event guilt.
The authors explicitly describe Study 3’s humanlikeness result as correlational. A significant indirect effect alone does not identify a causal mediator.
Some measures include responsibility- and accountability-related wording alongside guilt; interpretations depend on the operationalization.
Non-significant alternative-mediator measures do not prove that empathy, detectability or other mechanisms are absent in all real retail settings.
Study 2 reports a significant AI-versus-machine intention contrast but a non-significant guilt contrast; keep the outcome distinctions rather than summarize every contrast as significant or null.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The broader review describes mixed success of humanization in cooperation. These retail-intention associations are context-specific and do not overturn those limits or establish a universal intervention.

deferred.reason: Retain as a context-dependent proposed mechanism/application within the existing machine-penalty evidence, not a duplicate broad interaction effect.

deferred.term: Norm Activation model; Negative State Relief model; Computers as Social Actors
deferred.reason: Background frameworks, not newly demonstrated behaviours in this paper. Their cited primary sources have not been independently read here.

limitations: One new human construct is indexed with an explicitly untested AI analogue.
The study does not demonstrate that AI itself experiences guilt or commits the retail misconduct being rated.
